newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africa National Party to sue over truth battle.
newsitem.headline: S.Africa National Party to sue over truth battle.

text.p: South Africa's white-dominated National Party said on Thursday it was going to court in a battle with the "truth commission" probing human rights abuses under apartheid.

The Truth and Reconciliation Commission earlier rejected a demand by the opposition National Party (NP) for commission chairman Archbishop Desmond Tutu to apologise for public criticism he levelled at the party.

"Although our client is in favour of settling disputes through negotiations, the commission's intransigence in respect of the fundamental issues leaves our client with no option but to proceed with its court application," the NP's lawyers said in a statement.
The National Party, which implemented apartheid in 1948 and began dismantling it four decades later, began a boycott of the commission last month in protest at what it called biased treatment.

It objected to remarks by Tutu and Alex Boraine, his deputy, to the effect that party leader F.W. de Klerk had failed to fully accept that the NP's policies during the apartheid years were responsible for gross human rights abuses.
The party demanded an apology from Tutu and the resignation of Boraine, threatening legal action if the demands were not met.
Tutu, in a statement issued after a meeting of the commission on Thursday, said an urgent meeting should be held with de Klerk's party to resolve the conflict between them.
"The view of the full commission is that the demands cannot be acceded to," Tutu said.

"The commission believes that if dialogue could bring about a constitutional settlement in South Africa, it should be able to resolve the current difficulties," he said, adding that the truth body would be available for a meeting in Cape Town until Friday.

The truth commission was set up in 1995 to probe human rights abuses by all sides during apartheid, in the hope that revealing the truth would help to heal the wounds of the past and promote reconciliation.
